title: The more
hookLine: always the more, the greater good

lines: FOR THE GREATER GLORY OF GOD.
cards: Four letters sit at the top of homework pages in some Jesuit schools, written before the student's name: A, M, D, G. They stand for a Latin motto of the Jesuits, ad maiorem Dei gloriam, for the greater glory of God.
Notice the word in the middle. Not for the glory of God; for the greater glory. There's a comparison built into it, a reaching.
Jesuits pulled that reaching out into a single Latin word you'll hear in their schools, retreats and homilies. It fits on a wristband, and it's easy to get badly wrong.

teach.b: Magis. Latin for more. It shows up at the very end of the foundation in the Exercises, where Ignatius says we should desire and choose only what leads more to the end for which we are made.
Not just a good choice: the choice that leads further toward God. Some readers hear that little comparison again and again in the Exercises. Here's the trap.

teach.h: WHAT LEADS MORE TO OUR END.
teach.b: Heard carelessly, magis sounds like more hours, more projects, more achievement, more pressure. A Jesuit motto for burnout. That's not what Ignatius means.
The more is measured against one thing only: the love and service of God and neighbor.
Sometimes the magis is doing more. Sometimes it's doing less, better. Sometimes it's resting, because a tired person loves badly.
Sometimes it's saying no to a good thing to make room for a better one. That's why magis lives beside yesterday's cura personalis and the indifference from earlier in the Exercises. It's not a whip.
It's a question asked with open hands: of the good options in front of me, which leads more toward love?
Jesus describes his own purpose with a kind of more, in the Douay-Rheims of John's Gospel: "I am come that they may have life, and may have it more abundantly." Abundance, not exhaustion.
In a plain week, magis might mean making the phone call instead of sending the text, reading the bedtime story slowly, spending five extra minutes to do a task well.
Or closing the laptop, because the more for tonight is sleep.

how: Jesuit schools and retreats speak of the magis as choosing what leads more to God's glory and the good of others; some students write AMDG, the Jesuit motto, at the top of their work.

o: the Latin name for a Jesuit school's top honor
always adding more hours and more work for God
the choice that leads more toward God and neighbor

p: for the greater glory of God

s: the magis means always doing more work
it's measured against love of God and neighbor. sometimes the more is less, or rest.
the Jesuit motto says for the greater glory of God, not just for the glory
ad maiorem Dei gloriam: the comparison is built in.
the magis has nothing to do with the Exercises
the foundation asks us to choose only what leads more to the end for which we are made.

games.q: it's late. you could stay up and polish a project, or go to bed so you're kind to your family tomorrow. which is the magis?
o: always the project: more is more.
whichever leads more toward love, which might be sleep.
neither: the magis is only for big decisions.
games.why: the more is measured by love of God and neighbor, not by hours. some nights the greater good is rest.

practice: Think of something ordinary ahead of you, a meal, a message, a chore, and hold two versions side by side: the usual way, and a way with a little more love in it, more care or patience rather than more effort.
Then ask honestly whether the more, this time, might be less. If you pray, ask God to show you which.

wordCard.voice: Magis. Latin for more: in the Ignatian sense, the choice that leads more toward God and neighbor, which isn't always the busier one. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: more. ecclesiastical pronunciation; classical Latin says MAH-gis.

carryVoice: Your line: magis. The more is measured by love and service, not by hours. Until tomorrow.
